Joined by President of Griffin Structures John Hughes and ELS Architect Clarence Mamuyac, Sanen reported that because of “unforeseen conditions,” the community pool is now delayed well past its original target of June 2024. Additionally the most recent completion date of September 2024 has been pushed back even farther and no estimated date of completion has been offered. articles.text: I was up early on Sunday morning, September 11th. A busy day was ahead. The lead television news stories of the morning were of the motorcade carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II through Scotland and somber observances in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania commemorating the 21st anniversary of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. Both stories served as reminders that grief and gratitude are frequent traveling companions. There was an outpouring of grief from people around the globe upon the death of the 96-year-old Queen of England. In Scotland, people lined the roadways as her coffin passed. With the grief there were also many expressions of gratitude for her fidelity to her work, her years as a global leader, her humor and her delight in her four-legged friends. As the motorcade carrying her coffin traversed the Scottish countryside, it was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. At the sites of the September 11 attacks the dead were remembered, the first responders were honored, hymns were sung, prayers were offered, and speeches were made. All were fitting expressions of the profound grief of that day, the persistent grief that is with us still. Yet, with the grief, there was gratitude. There was gratitude for the courage, the compassion, the connecting which the tragedies evoked. There was gratitude for the rebuilding that has taken place. There was gratitude for the restoration that continues. It was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. In the biblical narrative, grief and gratitude frequently travel together. In the Psalms, expressions of grief often give way to songs of gratitude. Psalm 74 is an excellent example. articles.text: A camp where Scouting begins A group of children make arts and crafts by lantern light. If you’ve ever wondered if your child would enjoy Cub Scouts, you might want to consider this week’s Cub Scout Twilight Camp in Piedmont Park. Twilight Camp is a Cub Scout event held by the Piedmont Scout Council. From Tuesday through Thursday evening, October 24-26 from 6:30 to 8:00 p.m., Cub Scouts will have their first taste of fun activities designed for 1st and 2nd graders. Located at Piedmont Community Hall this year, campers will rotate through different activity stations each evening, making Halloween-themed crafts, eating homemade treats, and the highlight of the week – racing model boats in the Raingutter Regatta. Twilight Camp is open to all grade school age youth. “It’s an introduction to Cub Scouting,” said Program Director Eris Turner, a Piedmont native. “We typically advertise it to Cub Scouts, but it’s also open to anyone in the community. We have some minor Scouting elements in it, but also fun program things that kids might do at their Cub Scout Pack meetings.” Turner said that several families each year discover Scouting after attending Twilight Camp. “In addition, it’s a chance to have your kids be around other kids,” he added. Twilight Camp, he explained, is an “easy, low-commitment” way of trying out Scouting – perfect for parents and children who are considering getting involved. articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church invites the community to a presentation of a Requiem Mass for All Souls on Wednesday, November 1, at 6:30 p.m. Ben Bachmann, Director of Music, will lead an orchestra and St. Paul’s Choir in a performance of the majestic Requiem in D minor, Op. 48, by Gabriel Fauré. The California Department of Education’s results, released on October 18, are shown below. Overall, over 86% of Piedmont students met or exceeded state standards in English Language Arts – a one percent drop from 2022. articles.text: Amid discussions about negotiations between the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) and the Piedmont Association of Teachers, members of the PUSD School Board have a message. “To our educators - we hear you and we see you. We want the best for our educators, our students and our community. We have had countless hours of discussions about how we can fairly compensate our educators and we all agree that that is critical. We’ve discussed how to increase revenues. We’ve discussed cuts, we are reading your emails and we are working toward compensation,” said school board member Lindsay Thommason at the October 11 School Board meeting. Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign is one way to increase revenues, and the Giving Campaign team is urging the community to donate to help support teachers. “This year $2.3 million of PEF’s $3 million grant to PUSD, about 77%, is earmarked for instructional salaries,” confirmed Giving Campaign Co-Chair Kim Hunter, “The more money we raise, the more we can give.” The Giving Campaign raises money to fund teachers, intervention specialists, paraeducators, wellness, professional development, technology, and other activities that lead to PUSD student success. “When our budget is so extremely tight and we face really tough decisions, we’re looking for creative solutions. The Giving Campaign has a huge goal of $3.5 million but that doesn’t mean we can’t raise more than that. I would love to see our participation go up, especially as a sign of support for our amazing teachers. Every family should give to this important cause because we do have an amazing group of teachers. Please do your part by giving to the Giving Campaign.” said school board member Hilary Cooper The Piedmont Giving Campaign has raised over $1.5 million so far this year. The campaign’s goal is to raise another $2 million. “As part of the Superintendent’s Advisory Committee, I have been working on enrollment and looking at our peer schools, both public and private, at what the cost is of some of the private schools,” added Thomasson. For high school in particular it ranges from 45 to 60 thousand dollars per year. So, what the Giving Campaign is asking is less than one month’s tuition at a private school. This week, with free book tables at the Halloween parade, sugar skull making, and events for young children, the Piedmont Ave. Branch Library is sure to have a little bit of something for everyone in the community this Halloween season. The library will host several events related to the Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade on Saturday, October 28. Before the parade, visitors can join Storytime with Shani at 10 a.m. at Key Route Plaza, 41st and Piedmont Ave. Friends of Piedmont Ave. Library will staff a table there with free books and button-making. After the parade kids are invited to the library at 2 p.m. to make sugar skulls with their friends and library staff. Sugar skulls have their roots in Mexican cultural traditions and are typically used to decorate altars honoring ancestors during Día de los Muertos. Although the skulls are usually made out of cane sugar, library staff will be creating the skulls with modeling clay and then decorating them with glitter and other materials. In addition to participating in parade activities, the library will also have other programs throughout the month. Their Fall Stay & Play program is held every Tuesday at 10:15 a.m. For one hour each Tuesday, the library will provide a selection of toys and games for play. This program is aimed at children ages 18 months to 3 years, but kids of all ages are welcome. Meet the Manager The Piedmont Avenue Branch Library recently welcomed a new branch manager, Sabah Abdulla. A long-time resident of the neighborhood, she knows the library well. After missing two years of school as a teenager when her family had to return to Yemen, she had fallen behind in her studies. So, Sabah went to the Piedmont Avenue Branch Library every day to study and catch up. She always felt safe and welcome there. During college, Sabah worked part-time at several branches and she was encouraged by the amazing library staff to get her library degree. Sabah earned her MLS at San Jose State and immediately began working as a Teen Librarian at the Asian Branch Library. At the Piedmont Avenue Branch, Sabah is working to build back its programs: chess club, Baby Café, bringing books to seniors, among several. In the future, she plans to connect with neighborhood organizations to share the wonderful resources at the library. This year’s event honored the artistic legacy of former Artistic Director Robert Geary and accompanist and composer Susan Bohlin while raising funds for PEBCC programs, camps and tours. The event featured multiple compositions of Bohlin’s, including the world premiere of Song for Clea, a special piece she wrote for her youngest granddaughter. “Our season’s theme, Together We Belong, could not be a more apt description of Bob and Sue’s Piedmont Choirs celebrates 42 years of making music legacy and impact in the choirs,” said Executive Director Keri Butkevich. “From lifting up new voices to making sure young campers weren’t homesick, they and Founder Suzie Rahl have created a space where high artistry meets the great love that leads to lifelong connection. It is no wonder that we had alumni and past staff and families come from across the globe from all decades to celebrate them and the organization they shepherded with passion and commitment for four decades.” Bohlin retired from PEBCC after 39 years of exceptional service to the choirs. She has served as conductor, accompanist, theory director, festival manager, training department director, and Associate conductor of the performing department. Reflecting upon her time with the choirs, Bohlin mused, “I became aware of the extraordinary gift of life guidance through music education that PEBCC and their staff were providing for chorus members. articles.text: Girls team places 3rd, boys team 4th Piedmont’s cross country team returned to Oyster Bay Regional Park in San Leandro for its second league meet of the season on Wednesday, October 18. Xander Schulte-Sasse won the race with a best-ever time, and the girls’’ team placed third overall in a field of 10 teams. The PHS boys were fourth on a hot 90-degree day. To feel like I could step it up one more notch made me even more excited,” said Schulte-Sasse. The girls’ team was without senior Jamie Schwarz, who was preparing for today’s Mid-Season Mania 3200M Invitational at Campolindo. “Jamie was getting some much-needed rest in preparation for the end of the season races. Our varsity runners will be competing at Campolindo High School this Wednesday on the track in a 3,200 meter race,” explained Zirkelbach. Sophomore Skylar Best led the way for the girls’ team with a time of 19:31.25, placing fourth in a field of 72 runners. articles.text: In an emotional end to Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball season, the Highlanders lost 3-2 to Berkeley on Wednesday, October 18 after opening the match with a 2-0 lead, The Highlanders needed a win to qualify for the post-season North Coast Section playoffs and nearly upset this year’s League (Western Alameda County Conference) champions in dramatic fashion. In a match before a Piedmont home crowd, it all came down to a final 15-point fifth set tiebreaker. Piedmont held match point at 14-13 before Berkeley scored the game’s final three points to win the match and eliminated the Highlanders from post-season play. “I’ve had this group since they were freshmen, so watching them for four years has been a blessing… I think we got a little fatigued, some of us aren’t used to playing in this kind of environment. They did a really good job. It was such a hard loss because of how hard they tried. It’s been a really good season regardless of the outcome,” said coach Mariah Cardeñas. Piedmont entered the match with a 5-6 league record and needing the win to finish at .500 for an automatic bid to the NCS playoffs. The match marked an end to Sadie Town’s illustrious volleyball career at PHS. A three-year starter, Her total number of kills is likely the most by a player in the last decade. Her 28 kills against Bishop O’Dowd was the most by a Piedmont player since Samantha Fanger’s 24 in 2017. The team graduates a handful of players to graduation next spring: Bauer and Beck Peterson, Elena Stevens, Maddy Mullin, Molly Wagener, Maddy Hill, Izzy Grimmer and Town. Game Recap Piedmont came out hot in the first set, jumping out to a big 9-4 lead before extending to 12-6. Berkeley battled back to a 13-11 deficit, but PHS went on a 4-1 scoring run to make it 17-12. At 23-19, Piedmont closed out the set with a kill by Town by tapping a shot to an open spot on the floor, while Maddy Mullin slammed a crosscourt spike for the winner at 25-19. In the second set, with Berkeley holding an 8-7 lead, Piedmont went on a 7-3 scoring run to take Staff Photos Volleyball coach Mariah Cardeñas urges her team on during a heated five-set match against Berkeley. a 13-11 lead. That’s when the Highlanders scored six straight points with help of a kill by Molly Wagener, two aces by Kalindi Kim, and a block by Town. At 23-16, Piedmont’s Elena Stevens scored off a block before Berkeley blocked a shot of its own. The Jackets server sent a ball into net for a 25-17 Piedmont win. But from there, Piedmont’s offense couldn’t find the same power behind its shots. The Yellowjackets’ outside hitter, team captain Elle Walker, took over the game with 17 kills in the final three sets. In the third set, Piedmont got out to an 11-8 lead, but Berkeley stormed to the front with four straight points to make it 12-11. PHS regained the lead at 13-12 after an offensive error and an ace by Izzy Grimmer, but then Berkeley dominated the rest of the set Sadie Town with a kill against Berkeley. She wrapped up her Piedmont career as one of the best outside hitters in recent school history.

articles.text: More than 6 miles of hiking along Hayward Plunge Trail Happy Halloween! It’s the spooky season, so what better time to delve into haunted urban legends? Growing up around Hayward, the gruesome legend of the Hayward Plunge Trail at Green Belt Park is a well-known story, providing an eerie ghost hunt for teenagers at night. For those easily spooked, be advised that the story isn’t for the faint of heart. Allegedly, a swimming instructor at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool in the 1960s led his entire class of child-aged students up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting as a teenager of children in all-white garb from head-to-toe. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be entirely covered by thickets of California Bays, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the inner East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep downhill declines. It is considered a very technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding out of the ground. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to continue the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in the process through the hills of Green Belt Park. You’ll top out above the tree-line, you have the option to do a 180 and head back down, or turn right and walk straight down Durham Way to continue the loop onto the Greenbelt Hiking and Riding trail—which reunites you with Ward Creek until reaching Campus Drive. In the six miles of hiking, we only passed 29 people around noon on a Sunday, so less than five people per mile on a popular day for hikers. The trail is a great spot for a lower leg workout with over 1,100 feet in elevation gain. No ghost sightings were made, but perhaps my own paranoia brought out the feeling that eyes were always following me. Punch in “Hayward Plunge” or “Memorial Park Hayward” into your GPS device to access this trail’s parking lot. To cut off the first 1.3 miles, park on Campus Drive. This article was originally printed in the Piedmont Post in October 2020. You’ll pass over numerous bridges on your hike. The view of the Greenbelt trail next to Ward Creek connects with the Hayward Plunge Trail. The trail is wide, giving ample space for hikers and bikers.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Nollywood Dreams, a new comedy by Jocelyn Bioh, is playing onstage now through November 11. Set in Lagos, Nigeria in the 1990’s, the play follows Ayamma Okafor, played by Angel Adedokun, who dreams of stardom. She has her heart set on the bright lights of Nollywood, the burgeoning Nigerian film industry akin to California’s Hollywood an Calcutta’s Bollywood. She and her sister Dede, played by Brittany Nicole Sims, toil in their parents’ travel agency and unexpectedly audition with Nigeria’s best-known director as the story begins to unfold. The playwright hoped to capture a moment in time in Nigeria, one that most Western audiences don’t see, and blend it with comedic elements. “That’s an important goal for me,” Bioh told the San Francisco Chronicle. “I really am trying to diversify and break open people’s singular narrative of Africa and African stories. We learn about these people who inhabit the continent, and it allows us to have a more humanizing perspective on them.” The play is premiered October 4 at San Francisco Playhouse and is directed by Margo Hall. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/upcoming-plays/ to see showtimes and to purchase tickets. Ayamma (Angel Adedokun) works at her parents’ travel agency in the SF Playhouse production of Nollywood Dreams.

articles.text: Performances in Oakland on November 3-4 Oakland Ballet celebrates Dia de Los Muertos (Day of the Dead) with performances of “Luna Mexicana”on October 28 in San Jose and November 3 and 4 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is one of the Bay Area’s most elaborate and inclusive events for the Dia de Los Muertos holiday, which is celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico. It is a blend of exuberant and traditional dance, joyful music, vibrant costumes, flowers, candles, and food, and is a gathering for families and loved ones. The performance features the return of Viva la Vida, a ballet inspired by the life and spirit of Frida Kahlo. Luna Mexicana is co-choreographed by Martín Romero of Ballet Folklórico México Danza and Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig. Ballet Folklórico México Danza will present traditional Mexican Folkloric dance, and Mariachi Mexicanisimo will perform folk mariachi music. Performances at the Paramount Theater in Oakland will Oakland Ballet celebrates Dia de los Muertos October 28 to November 4. take place on Friday, November 3, at 7:30 p.m., and on Saturday, November 4, at Paramount Theater in Oakland. An earlier performance will be held at 2:30 p.m. on Saturday, October 28, at Hammer Theatre in San Jose. Visit www.oaklandballet.org to purchase tickets or call the box office at (510) 893-3132.

articles.text: The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra (SFMO) makes a return engagement with a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 11, its sixth concert at the Center in as many years. The Orchestra’s season theme this year is “Napoli and the Revolution.” “We chose this theme because the 18th century was a time of revolutionary thought,” explained Achille Bocus, musical director of SFMO “Across Europe and America enlightened ideas of freedom, order, rationality, and happiness influenced politics, art, and music. The music of the time reflected this, with the end of the Baroque and emergence of the Classical Period, and the birth of mandolin as a popular instrument in Naples. “It’s the music that Jefferson, Franklin, Paine and other revolutionaries would have heard.” The Orchestra will perform music from the late baroque and classical periods, including: • Johann Sebastian Bach: Selections from Art of the Fugue • Giuseppe Giuliano: Concerto for Mandolin in B flat (Achille Bocus, soloist) • Wolfgang Mozart: Selections from London Notebook Achille Bocus, musical director of San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra, will be the soloist in the Giuliano Concerto for Mandolin in B flat at concert on November 11 at Piedmont Center for the Arts. • Giovanni Battista Sammartini: Sinfonia in G Major for String Orchestra The family-friendly concert will begin at 5:00 p.m. on November 11. Admission is $20 general, $15 student/senior, and free for children 12 and under. Tickets may be purchased at the door, or at the Orchestra’s ticketing site: sfmandolin.square.site.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation, will present its Fall Concert on Saturday, November 4 at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. The orchestra will perform Roman Carnival Overture by Berlioz (1843). Rhapsody On A Windy Night by Cavaterra (2022), and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4 in F minor Op. 36 (1877). Tickets are $20 General admission, and free for students who register at (http://data.ypsomusic.org/tickets). Call (510) 849- 9776 for additional information. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is celebrating its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director and Conductor. The orchestra has 99 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from throughout the greater Bay Area. articles.text: Narrowly defined, a dilemma is a predicament in which two possibilities present themselves, both equally undesirable. The Dilemma certainly meets that criterion. Ronny (Vince Vaughn), in partnership with his best friend, Nick (Kevin James), is scouting for an appropriate place to propose to his girlfriend, Beth (Jennifer Connelly), when he spots Nick’s wife, Geneva (Winona Ryder), hungrily kissing another man. His problem is what to do with this information. What is his moral duty to Nick? And how will it impact their business? They are close to signing a contract with Dodge for a green engine that has the power and the amplification of a 66 Ford GT-350 or the iconic Dodge Hemi: in other words, it’s a muscle car with batteries. It’s a guy car we’re told by Ronny, not a lame, quiet, hybrid. Telling Nick about Geneva at this delicate moment could unhinge the deal by distracting Nick, the engineering genius behind the engine, and already stressed to the max by deadlines. Ergo: Ronny’s dilemma. The scene of observed infidelity takes place at the end of act one, an act that establishes that Ronny and Nick are involved in a long-term bromance. They’re straight, the movie emphasizes, but they’re also best buds: they go clubbing, play hockey, and share a love of cars. As act two begins, it would seem natural that Ronny would go home to Beth – she’s bright, a successful chef, caring, and eager to be included in whatever speed bumps Ronny might encounter. In fact, she was there for him as he overcame a gambling problem some years back. This is a woman who can be leaned on. Instead of sharing his dilemma with her, however, Ronny begins a long period of deception, dissembling, and even stalking. He faults Geneva for her lack of honesty, yet rejects honesty as perhaps the best modus operandi, at least with Beth. And thus the film Vince Vaughn and Kevin James in The Dilemma

articles.text: Simply do the math. As a nation we spent the better part of two centuries failing to recognize the talent and humanity of a people, their gifts, their intellect, their potential. It was called racism. The loss has been incalculable. Hidden Figures is the exhilarating true story, based on the book by Margot Lee Shetterly, about three black women who worked at NASA’s Langley facility, in Hampton, VA. during the late 50s and early 60s. The race into space had been joined. Russia had gotten America’s attention and we scrambled to catch up. These women – all profoundly talented – were, in the eyes of NASA, all but invisible. They worked for the agency during a time when it was segregated and sexist. There were separate bathrooms, dining rooms and work areas for “colored only” and for “whites only.” The barriers Katherine G. Johnson (Taraji P. Henson), Dorothy Vaughn (Octavia Spencer) and Mary Jackson (Janelle Monae’) faced were appalling and, in retrospect, all but impossible to comprehend. What is remarkable about the film is that it is unflinching in its depiction of the bigotry, both overt and covert, that greeted them each day at NASA. Until, finally it didn’t. At the center of the film is Katherine G. Johnson, a gifted mathematician, who is brilliant at geometric calculations. Gradually, her genius takes her to the center of the mission to launch astronauts into orbit. NASA clearly had the hardware. What it didn’t have were the calculations to not only reach space, but to bring the likes of John Glenn, who orbits earth, safely back. It’s at that intersection that Katherine Johnson steps forward. She can do the math that is absolutely essential. It’s deeply satisfying watching her overcome the prejudice and discrimination, What is surprising is that the men of NASA are incredibly well schooled engineers, and yet they are blind to their own bigotry. They don’t see Katherine or her precocious gift. They see only color. But against all odds, the trio – Johnson, Vaughn and Jackson – persevere: they push back, they bend rules until finally NASA begins to see them not as black women but as individuals who have a great deal to offer. What is also wonderful about Hidden Figures is that the narrative includes moments when the women are at home, at picnics, at church, surrounded by children and husbands, who all view what they do as groundbreaking, and filled with pride and satisfaction. The film opens in a delightful way: the three women are stopped on a Virginia highway on the way to work after their car breaks down, with Katherine Johnson lying underneath the car to check the starter motor. Unexpectedly a local police officer pulls up and asks to see some I.D. They each show him their NASA badges and he looks at them with obvious disbelief and then says, with a shake of his head, “I didn’t know that NASA hired… women.” Indeed it did. And that decision was how we managed to get John Glenn home safely. Hidden Figures. Directed by Theodore Melfi. Starring Tara R. Henson, Octavia Spencer, Janelle Monae. 2 hrs., 7 min. Rated PG. articles.text: A scene from Transformers: Dark of the Moon In most big tent blockbuster films – CGI driven, saturated with action – there is always a tension between spectacle and story. Generally, in movies of this ilk, plot and dialogue are given short shrift and spectacle prevails. If this trend persists, Michael Bay, director of T3, will dismiss the screenwriter and offer his films as experiences, absent any exposition at all. But no worries, action scenes that fill the screen to bursting with overwhelming energy and sound are Michael Bay’s specialty, and T3 is all about extraordinary moments that are can’tlook-away engaging. There may be no better vehicle for Bay’s particular brand of movie than one in which the characters are machines. Seriously. That doesn’t mean he doesn’t want his audience to identify with these giant Hasbro created Bots which were all the rage in the 80s. He does. Hence, they are nicely anthropomorphized, with individual personalities, well spoken. The good Bots (Autobots) and the bad Bots (Decepticons) have movie star blue eyes and satanic red eyes respectively. They also possess other humanoid qualities – interesting facial features, massive arms, tree trunk legs, hands (prehensile? probably not), all wonderfully and magically articulated – which makes them as interesting as the humans. In fact, Optimus Prime and Bumblebee have more heart than many of the humans. Regarding humanizing animals and Bots, it’s something that resonates, requiring little suspension of disbelief, and is essential to creating a relationship between the Bots and the audience. Disney divined this at the outset, creating grainy cartoons starring Mickey and Donald and later the memorable Bambi. If you’re a Transformer aficionado, you’re well versed in the backstory of Sam Witwicky (Shia LaBeouf) and the Bots, all explained in the first Transformers movie. It was the best of the three; far more interesting, long on character development, and fresh in its dialogue and premise and opening set up. In T3, not so much. Sam does have a new hottie, Carly (ex-model Rosie Huntington-Whiteley), whose derriere is introduced before she is, and who needs saving. A lot of saving. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Something Borrowed is all about triangulation. But then triangles are a staple of romantic comedies; in fact, they’re a staple of the human experience. Triangulation is familiar behavior involving three people, two are on the inside of a situation or issue or complaint and one is on the outside, essentially unaware. Triangles can be wicked. And they can be a source of endless comedic situations, which is why Hollywood writers return so often to this particular well. They have tapped that well in Something Borrowed. Darcy (Kate Hudson) and Rachel (Gennifer Goodwin) are best friends forever. They are also opposites. Darcy is a bit shallow and self-absorbed, as well as spontaneous and glowing. Rachel is down-to-earth, hardworking, a lawyer. She also finds it incredibly difficult to tell Darcy what it is she wants. And what she wants, with all her heart, is fellow law school study partner, Dex (Colin Egglesfield). When Darcy, Dex and Kate meet for drinks, and Darcy settles her strobe light gaze on Dex, she asks Rachel if she would mind if Dex asks her out. Rachel, her heart yearning to declare her real feelings for Dex, lies and insists that she and Dex are just good friends. As a result, she hands Dex to Darcy, masking her deep reluctance as well as sadness. And so. the triangle is constructed. What happens next gets complicated, then more complicated, as Rachel and Dex, like two magnets, are drawn to each other despite the impending wedding being planned for Darcy and Dex. All of this is part of the set up. Rachel’s other BBF is Ethan Kate Hudson and Colin Egglesfield in Something Borrowed

articles.text: It was a night all will recall, dripping with nostalgia and sentiment as the semi-retired MTT returned to conduct Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony. With the elderly, ailing podium laureate back, the tributes by the full house were never more pronounced. Yes, a love-in, by any measure. And with not one but two wars raging on the far side of Earth, never were Beethoven’s choral messages of hope, “All men will be brothers,” with the following “Be embraced, ye millions,” more needed. The messages struck home to the heart. No mere concert, this was a night to remember, with the imposing SFS Chorus’ 110-plus members outdoing themselves in the exuberant finale to cap the 75-minute performance. Shuffling on and off the stage with halting steps, Michael Tilson Thomas appeared to be the most beloved music director here since World War Two. Who else would have been honored with an eight-minute (!) standing ovation at the end, silenced only when the maestro withdrew to the wings for the last time, solicitously led by the singers. Else the sell-out crowd at Davies might still be clapping. His conducting was not lax, but rather relaxed – soulful and low-key, with a personalized that unprecedented choral finale. And that finale was glorious, doing something I hadn’t heard at the SFSC in three decades: pronouncing the consonants, so that the printed German texts could be followed. Credit the new SFSC director Jenny Wong for the warmly welcomed improvement as she too was celebrated by MTT at the conclusion. The finale had a robust launching by baritone Dashon Burton, who set the rafters ringing, followed by a consistent set of soloists: tenor Ben Bliss, soprano Angel Blue and mezzo Tamara Mumford. MUSIC NOTES The shorter companion piece scheduled, Shango Memory by the late Berkeley black composer and professor Olly Wilson, was dropped without explanation… MTT, 78, was diagnosed with aggressive brain cancer during the pandemic. He had retired as music director in 2020, after 25 years at the helm…The choral texts came from poetry by Friedrich Schiller (1759-1805), who, like the SFS, must have had a crystal ball to foresee how timely his texts would be at this very moment in history. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, also contributes reviews of the Bay Area classical concert scene on the web site www. artsSF.com. Michael Tilson Thomas, retired Music Director of San Francisco Symphony baton beat that only these veteran SFS players could read and respond to. Their affection, too. was palpable, as with the ensemble’s amiable chuckles when violist Jonathan Vinocour had to leap up to help him with his printed score, to the maestro’s gratitude. And again, during the plaudits, when his players donned bluerimmed glasses out of nowhere, matching his own. If the trumpets and timpani were unflinchingly zealous October 19, no one could miss the delicacy of the Scherzo, the silky strings in the Adagio with the eloquent woodwind ensemble, or the superior cellos leading into Violinist and composer Niccolo Paganini. playing while in prison. articles.text: Visit the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco to see its newest exhibition on view, Takashi Murakami: Unfamiliar People – Swelling of Monsterized Human Ego, on display now through February. Murakami: Monsterized is the first solo exhibition in San Francisco by Japanese artist Murakami, born in 1962. He is an internationally recognized contemporary artist and major figure in global pop culture, whose influences draw from the aesthetic characteristics of the Japanese artistic tradition and the nature of postwar Japanese culture. Murakami’s influence in the contemporary art world makes his works highly sought-after in art trades, and his vibrant prints maintain a consistently high value. In this exhibition, the artist’s larger-than-life paintings and sculptures use monsters, a common theme in his pieces, as a central motif. Senior Curator of Japanese Art Laura Allen said, “The visual DNA of Murakami’s characters has origins in centuries-old styles in Japanese art, such as depicting Buddhist arhats and Daoist immortals as wizened beings with strange features, bulging eyes, and bared teeth.” Murakami has added “technicolor palette, goofy expressions, and eclectic mixture of motifs” that quickly became his trademark, Allen added. Murakami: Monsterized is open an extra hour until 6 p.m. Friday through Monday and until 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Visit https:// asianart.org/ to learn more.

The wines of Cahors will not remind you of Argentina but instead of Bordeaux. Cahors is influenced by the Mediterranean as well as by the Atlantic, and although winters are colder than in Bordeaux, the wines tend to be more concentrated. Du Cedre began the transition to organic farming in the 1990’s and they were certified fully organic in 2021. The Tour des Gendres Winery in Bergerac in the Dordogne River Valley of France Clos de Gamot is a traditional old-school producer of wines. serves, sparked by herbal and earthy hints supported with a firm, grainy texture, and finishing with gorgeous freshness. This wine is built to last for decades in the cellar. Chateau Tour des Gendres I visited this winery 30 years ago when Luc Conti oversaw the place. It is not in Cahors but farther north in Bergerac in the Dordogne River valley. The Conti family originally settled in the area in the 1920s, began planting vines in 1984 and making wine in 1986. On my return visit this year I was greeted by Luc’s daughter Margaux and Gilles Conti owners of Tour des Gendres Margaux and her brother Gilles who are now the winemaker and estate manager. I was drawn to the place on my first visit because I loved a wine they produced from Semillon and Sauvignon Blanc that was aged in new oak barrels that gave it a powerful oaky vanilla nose. The wine philosophy has changed dramatically as I heard disparaging comments about both new oak and the Semillon grape. Things have not gone downhill as the new wines that were poured were full of character and delicious. They started with Cantalouette rouge and blanc that were refreshing quaffers that they served slightly chilled. Both were clean, savory and satisfying and at $11 a bottle are a great bang for the buck. They went on to pour a nice 100% Merlot called Les Gendres and a 100% Cabernet Franc called Les Anciens Francs, both excellent representatives of the varietals. Tour des Gendres is imported by Martine’s Wines of Novato. • Favorite Wine – 2021 Tour des Gendres “Le Vif” Finding this wine was a delightful surprise as it is made from the Savagnin grape which is not usually found outside its native region of The Jura in France. It had a charming nose of honeysuckle and peaches, great body of melon, apricot fruit and minerals with layers of complexity. It reminded me of a first class Savennieres from the Loire Valley. While delicious now, this wine has the potential to improve in the cellar for a decade. Tour des Gendres VIF is made from the Savagnin grape.

The group was pleased to welcome Don Fones who was walking with the group for the first time. There was a good turnout of 37 walkers and one K-9 best friend for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays gathering on October 18. The group had scheduled its annual pre-Halloween walking tour of Mountain View Cemetery for the following week and wanted to get into the Halloween spirit by looking for Halloween house decorations around the city. The group went to the lesswalked, block-long Sierra Avenue, and right away on the corner was their first Halloween sighting. In front of a house was a strange looking scarecrow with a metallic wrap exterior that looked a little like Big Bird. It was explained that this was one of the scarecrows that Piedmont elementary school students made for the Piedmont Harvest Festival. Each class creates a scarecrow out of recycled materials, and they are auctioned off as a fundraiser for the schools. After Sierra they went on Sheridan Avenue to Lakeview Avenue and climbed to the top at Sea View Avenue where they saw a larger-than-life sized ghost in front of a house. Further down Sea View, the front yard of one beautiful home had been taken over by a set of even scarier Halloween characters. The worst/ best of them was a smiling, Joker-style clown popping out of a Jack-in-the-box. He was surrounded by skeletons and ghouls emerging from the ground. They were quite a sight at 11 in the morning. The group made their way down Sea View to Hampton Road and the towards Glen Alpine Road, where they saw a wonderful historic mansion, Hampton House, designed by noted architect Albert Farr in 1926. In front, it had a set of life-size, playful, inflatable Halloween characters. There were dragons, ghost dogs, an octopus, a skeleton riding on a motorcycle, and several others. The walkers stopped briefly for a group photo. It was noted that the home is currently for sale for $14,850,000. It has eight bedrooms, nine baths, and is 11,870 square feet with a tennis court, a rose garden, mature hedges and trees, and a separate guest unit. The temperature was starting to rise, so the group thought it would be smart to start back before it got too hot. On their way back to the center of town, they passed Hampton Field, went down La Salle Avenue and onto Indian Road, where they passed more Halloween decorations. This Halloween house sightseeing was a fun way for the walkers to start their countdown to the always enjoyable tour of Mountain View Cemetery one week later – and also to get ready for all the wonderful, little trick or treaters at the end of the month. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Piedmont Real Estate Update October 2023 The Impact of Rising Interest Rates on Real Estate and the Economy The unprecedented surge in interest rates in 2022 and 2023 and the impact on the real estate market have ignited discussions in housing and financial circles. This month’s newsletter explores key elements of this conversation and how it affects the consumer. Interest Rates, Inflation, and the Jobs Report The September Jobs Report exceeded expectations by adding 336,000 new jobs, putting pressure on the Federal Reserve to consider another interest rate hike. As we have seen in real time over the past year, interest rates play a critical role in shaping the economy and housing market by influencing borrowing costs and investment decisions. While we don’t yet know if the Fed will go through with another increase, the real estate, building, and mortgage industries have been vocal about what another hike means for the ability to build, buy, or sell real estate. The Federal Reserve's historic efforts to combat inflation began with a series of interest rate hikes, which pushed mortgage rates above 7% and abruptly slowed down the booming pandemic-driven housing market. According to forecasts by researchers at the San Francisco Federal Reserve, we might be on the brink of experiencing the most significant decline in shelter inflation since the Global Financial Crisis of 2007 to 2009. (Source: CNN) Rolling Recession Rising interest rates can contribute to a recession by increasing borrowing costs, potentially reducing consumer spending, business investments, and housing demand. Gary Keller, co-founder of Keller Williams, has warned of a “rolling recession” that may affect different industries at different times in specific ways. Locally, residential real estate sales have slowed notably year over year, and prices are down 15-20% off of their highs in spring 2022. The complex relationship between Federal Reserve interest rate decisions and the economy affects various industries differently. The real estate sector, in particular, grapples with the impact of these rate hikes and their implications for housing market stability. It’s essential to stay informed as economic conditions evolve. Federal Reserve’s Interest Rate Hikes The Fed’s decision to raise interest rates has evoked mixed responses. While intended to curb inflation and ensure economic stability, critics fear it may slow down borrowing, investment, and spending, harming the real estate market and the overall economy. Comparing Interest Rates To put the interest rate changes in perspective, in 2022, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was around 3.0%, while in 2023, it rose to approximately 3.5%. For a million-dollar loan, this equates to an annual difference of $5,000 in interest payments.
